direction calculations.

A complex number a+bi represents a point (a,b)
in a plane. Its horizontal

coordinate is the real part and its vertical
coordinate is the coefficient of i.

The point with x coordinate two and y
coordinate one is 2+i.

Multiplying by i gives 2i+i squared, which
equals minus one plus 2i.

The new x coordinate is minus one and the new
y coordinate is two. The arrow turns

ninety degrees counterclockwise while
retaining length square root of five.

Multiplying a point (a,b) by i changes it to
(-b,a),

allowing multiplication to represent a planar
turn.

In three dimensions, we also need an axis that
defines the rotation plane.

We will extend this direction calculation to a
quaternion using that axis.

This quaternion lecture has two episodes.
After outlining the complete journey,

this first episode explains how to construct a
stored rotation and undo it.

How can four numbers record an airborne
rotation in a game?
We will observe ski and bike orientations,

then visualize the four quaternion components
and their half-angle.
We will undo and compose rotations,

and compute the difference between two
orientations.
Finally, we will check sign and normalization

pitfalls and rotate a vector in a worked
exercise.

Alongside skiing, we compare aircraft and
assembled components.

Identify what changes and what remains the
same.

Our goal is to record the body's orientation
at one instant.

Let us first distinguish where the rider is
from how the body is turned.

This is skiing in Riders Republic. Watch the
tilt of the body and skis.

Read forward movement separately from changes
in body orientation.

In the air, the travel path continues while
facing and bank also change.

Remaining near screen center does not imply an
unchanged orientation; the camera follows too.

We are learning a representation that can
describe the visible motion,

without claiming to have inspected the game
code.
Our next diagram will hold position fixed and

rotate the three body axes to isolate
orientation.

To understand this approach to rotation
through multiplication,

we first extend the number system. The square
of a real number is nonnegative,
so no real number squares to minus one.

We define a new rule in which i squared is
minus one.

The number i defined this way is called the
imaginary unit.

This rule does not make an imaginary number a
hidden object inside the game.

It provides a useful numerical tool for
direction calculations.

To see why it helps with rotation, we will
represent these numbers as point coordinates.

A complex number a+bi represents a point (a,b)
in a plane. Its horizontal

coordinate is the real part and its vertical
coordinate is the coefficient of i.

The point with x coordinate two and y
coordinate one is 2+i.

Multiplying by i gives 2i+i squared, which
equals minus one plus 2i.

The new x coordinate is minus one and the new
y coordinate is two. The arrow turns

ninety degrees counterclockwise while
retaining length square root of five.

Multiplying a point (a,b) by i changes it to
(-b,a),

allowing multiplication to represent a planar
turn.

In three dimensions, we also need an axis that
defines the rotation plane.

We will extend this direction calculation to a
quaternion using that axis.

We verified that multiplying by i produces a
ninety-degree turn.
How can we represent other angles?

Recall the unit circle from high-school
trigonometry. A unit arrow turned by

theta has horizontal component cos(theta) and
vertical component sin(theta).

Multiplication by cos(theta)+i sin(theta)
therefore rotates the plane by theta.

At ninety degrees the cosine is zero and the
sine is one, giving i.

This planar calculation uses the full physical
angle theta.

When the three-dimensional quaternion later
uses a half-angle,

we will compare the different operation
applied to the vector.
We learned about a planar angle.
Observe the red torso line.
Three dimensions require an axis too.

We now connect it to the three axis
components.

In a plane, two numbers and multiplication
could turn a direction. Extending that

idea to three dimensions requires choosing an
axis; let us examine the numbers we need.

A scalar means one number. Here a vector is a
three-number group describing a direction,

and a component is an individual number in
that group.

The symbols i,j,k belong to the
three-dimensional rotation algebra.

We do not need to draw a fourth physical
direction to store four numbers.

For a z-axis rotation, x and y are zero while
w and z carry angle information.

These are not four independent rotation
angles.
Which values produce 90 degrees?

We will construct them using a unit axis and
familiar trigonometry.

A quaternion contains one scalar and a
three-component vector.
We write components in w,x,y,z order.

A unit rotation quaternion has squared
components summing to one,
leaving three continuous degrees of freedom.

Four numbers are not four rotation angles, and
x,y,z are not Euler angles.

The algebra uses i,j,k, whose squares each
equal minus one.

The product ij is k, whereas ji is minus k: an
early hint that order matters.

A library may store x,y,z,w instead. Check the
named components and memory order.

Read the direction represented by three
components through the wings.

This excerpt changes from bicycle travel to
flight.
The red line joins the visible wing tips.

Compare it with the teal screen-horizontal
reference.

The camera also moves, so this projected angle
is not a world rotation angle.

How do we construct four components from an
axis and angle independent of the camera?

We have separated the roles of the four
components.

Now we need to construct them from the axis
and angle introduced in the preceding lesson.

Recall a unit axis and the angle of rotation
about it.
The scalar is cos of the half-angle,

and the vector is the unit axis times sin of
the half-angle.

At zero angle, cos is one and sin is zero,
giving the identity [1,0,0,0].

A 90-degree z rotation uses a 45-degree
half-angle, so w and z are both sqrt(2)/2.

The half-angle does not mean half the physical
rotation.

Multiplication on both sides produces the full
angle.

We retain right-handed column-vector
conventions,
and use radians in trigonometric calculations.

A planar rotation used sine and cosine of the
full angle,

but our quaternion uses 45 degrees for a
90-degree turn. This needs an explanation.

The difference is how we later apply it: the
rotation value multiplies

the vector on the left, and its inverse
multiplies it on the right.

The complete two-sided operation produces the

A one-sided intermediate is not a physical

A rotation changes their directions together

Applying the same ninety-degree model rotation

Skis, aircraft, ship parts and assembled

orientation problems despite their different

Multiply the z90 quaternion by itself,

The new scalar is the product of scalars minus

The two cross scalar-vector terms sum to a z
